title: AI's Frontrunners Are Just Refineries, Not the Native-App Winners
dek: AI has entered the agent stage: the first-stage leaders are just refineries, not the native-app winners; new platforms don't come from old platforms; organizations must shift from jobs to tasks; and in the end, what people compete on is the creativity to conjure something from nothing.
why: Zeng Ming uses a three-stage industrial history to give you a coordinate system for judging where AI stands — an antidote to the optimism of "this time is different," and a look at the opportunity window for application founders plus a brutal forecast for incumbents' transformation.
who: CEOs working on AI strategy, executives at traditional giants hunting for a second curve, AI investors, and technical founders torn between building models and building applications.
skip: The rapid-fire Q&A and book list at the end can be skipped (after 2:29).

points.h: Building agents today is like building websites in 1992
points.body: Zeng Ming divides the industrialization of general-purpose technology into three stages: first it becomes social infrastructure, then applications explode, and finally native applications emerge. In 2026, token as a unit of measurement reached consensus, showing the first stage has matured; the agent events around Chinese New Year (commonly called "lobster") marked AI's formal entry into the agent stage. He draws an analogy to the 1992 website-building movement: people then built websites to share information, today they build agents to share capabilities. The browser hasn't appeared yet, and whoever can establish agent standards and seize the user entry point may be the biggest opportunity of the next two years.

points.h: A ten-trillion-dollar company will appear, but not these two
points.body: Zeng Ming says bluntly that OpenAI and Anthropic are remarkable technological and commercial achievements, but business history shows the first wave of breakout companies is most likely not the big winners of the native-application stage. Yahoo reached a $120 billion market cap five years after founding, AOL was valued at $220 billion, and neither became the Google of the next era. Model companies are more like AI cloud companies, refineries that refine crude oil — the real application value belongs to chemical plants and car companies, and cars were not built by oil companies. He believes a ten-trillion-dollar company will certainly appear, but not necessarily the two current frontrunners. Model companies will evolve into a mature business of oligopoly plus heavy government regulation.

points.h: The unit of an AI-native organization is the task, not the job
points.body: The company corresponds to the industrial-age hierarchy; AI overturns the industrial age, and the corporate system will decline. The basic unit of an AI-native organization is not the job but the task: people are not organized by reporting lines but flow around "what problem needs solving," and humans and AI coordinate around tasks. Thus well-designed jobs and hierarchies will disappear, traditional middle management will die out, and future founders must first define the organization's task network. Silicon Valley's NewLab is a prototype of the new organizational form; OpenAI itself is more like a Lab than a traditional company. The culture of the new organization is more like a sports team, emphasizing transparency, sharing, and co-creation, no longer relying on commands and evaluations.

points.h: Excellence can only be judged in hindsight; being outstanding is visible on the spot
points.body: Zeng Ming argues that "outstanding ≠ excellent." Being outstanding is growth that continuously receives positive feedback, while excellence requires overcoming negative feedback again and again, persisting when everyone disapproves, and ultimately proving with huge success that you were the era's prophet — so "excellence is judged in hindsight." Outstanding people easily fall into a cycle of proving themselves, leading to conservative strategies. Excellent people have a small ego, tend to attribute success to the times and partners, and are driven by mission rather than external valuation. When identifying founders, he asks, "What kind of self will you be satisfied with ten years from now?" If the answer is "to build a ten-billion-dollar company," that is mainly ego-driven, not an inner mission. Truly excellent founders are often altruistic and empathetic.

points.h: Strategy in the AI era cannot be planned, only generated
points.body: Strategy in the AI era is not planning but generation. Zeng Ming proposes a "strategy generation system": the organization must build an environment and network where strategic insights emerge naturally. Because decision frequency is higher and quality demands are greater, the CEO cannot rely on linear extrapolation for planning, nor can strategy be outsourced to McKinsey — McKinsey's explosion was a product of the slow maturity of the industrial age. His methodology is "look ten years ahead, think three years ahead, act one year ahead," with the core being "think three years ahead": you must at least see two or three milestones, creating tension between short-term actions and the mid-term picture. Organizational building must ensure a sufficiently large context rather than control, letting the right people make the right decisions at the right time.

points.h: The right analogy for robots is electrical appliances, not cars
points.body: Zeng Ming believes robots are still in a strategic exploration phase, far from convergence. There are currently two paths — building a generalized brain first or building a scenario closed loop first — both logically valid, and it's impossible to judge in advance which is faster. By historical analogy, the auto industry had thousands of companies from 1900 to 1920, and only entered scale after Ford built the assembly line in 1913; robots have yet to reach their Model T moment, and whoever truly sells ten thousand robots first is already remarkable. But a better analogy for robots is electrical appliances rather than cars: after electricity was invented, countless categories appeared — refrigerators, washing machines, air conditioners — and robots interacting in the physical world will have N kinds of large scenarios; home, companionship, and industrial uses may each produce their own native giants.

points.h: The giants who feel safe are the least safe
points.body: Zeng Ming says that in the face of a giant wave, no one is safe; feeling safe is the most unsafe. In business history, no era's companies have smoothly transitioned to the next era; IBM and Microsoft are the only two possible exceptions, and both are full of uncertainty. AI is a productivity revolution that overturns the industrial revolution, not a continuity innovation like mobile internet, so old giants' technology reserves and organizational culture are negative assets. Google can live on as an AI cloud company but may not capture the consumer entry point; ByteDance has an AI cloud opportunity, but Doubao is not the future application; Tencent's social relationships will be restructured; Alibaba is likewise not naturally safe. New platforms will most likely be created by new companies.

points.h: Human value lies in creating from nothing, not writing songs or painting
points.body: Drawing on Drucker's framework, Zeng Ming defines the AI era as the era of creativity: all knowledge work that can be structured will be taken over by AI, and humans are both forced and finally liberated to develop new potential. That potential is called creativity — not writing songs or painting, but the ability to originally define complex problems and conjure something from nothing. AI has already taken away all existing knowledge; human value lies in creating what does not yet exist. So he calls his mission "to be a happy researcher," and believes civilization will reorganize around creativity next, even the education system will be forced to shift from "knowledge indoctrination" to "open exploration," because young people already know the old path has no way out.

An operating system that can directly dispatch all agents to complete tasks according to intent; Zeng Ming believes it belongs to the third stage and cannot yet be implemented.
A new organizational form dissatisfied with the corporate system, centered on researchers; OpenAI is seen as the earliest example.
A Silicon Valley buzzword meaning taking control of one's own destiny and actively seeking tasks and growth, replacing hierarchical command-driven work.
A management philosophy: provide ample shared context and information so members can make correct decisions autonomously.

quotes.text: The most successful companies are certainly contrarian, but being contrarian does not guarantee success.
It may not survive to the end. It will likely do well later on, but it is most likely not the big player, the big winner, of the native-application stage.
First-stage companies rarely survive to the second stage, and second-stage companies rarely survive to the third stage.

So companies will disappear, companies will die out. There's nothing to regret about that. There will be more fun things in the future — how many people are happy going to work at a company now? Not happy.

My technology is so advanced, I've created so much value, why might my company be worthless? Because of the basic laws of economics: as long as there is homogeneous supply, you cannot capture high profits, and you are a company that isn't worth much.

Excellence is judged in hindsight, because you overcame negative feedback again and again, and when everyone disapproved of you, you ultimately proved with huge success that you were the era's earliest prophet.
I have always felt that in the face of a giant wave, no one is safe; whoever feels safe is the least safe.
